name: Santos Dumont Airport
before:
Rio's city airport, right beside the financial district, and the one to book when a client is working rather than sightseeing. Since 2023 it has been largely domestic, with Galeão taking the international flights, and it remains one of the ten busiest airports in Brazil.

Access could hardly be simpler. The Rio de Janeiro Light Rail has a terminal station at the airport, linking it to downtown, the metro, the Central Railway Station and the Central Bus Station.

It is also one of the more interesting airports in Brazil to look at. The whole site was reclaimed from Guanabara Bay in 1934, replacing a seaplane terminal at Calabouço Point, and opened under its present name on 30 November 1936. The 1937 Pan American seaplane terminal still stands, modelled on the company's Miami building, and the passenger terminal begun in 1938 was designed by the MMM Roberto brothers after Paris Le Bourget.

It is named after Alberto Santos Dumont, the Brazilian aviation pioneer.
after:
Rio's city airport, right in the centre and the one to book when a client is working rather than sightseeing. Its scheduled flights are domestic, mostly short and medium-haul; international flights use Galeão. A federal limit on passenger numbers has applied since 2024, and it handled 6.2 million passengers in 2025. Infraero, the state airport company, runs it.

Access could hardly be simpler. The VLT light rail starts here, with connections to the metro at Cinelândia and Carioca, suburban trains at Central and the Rodoviária coach station.

Work began in 1934 on reclaimed land at Calabouço Point, and the airport opened as Santos Dumont on 30 November 1936. Its original terminal, designed by the Roberto brothers and opened in 1945, is a landmark of Brazilian modern architecture, listed since 1998.

It is named after Alberto Santos Dumont, the Brazilian aviation pioneer.

claims.note: Was 'Since 2023 it has been largely domestic'. It has been restricted to domestic flights since a 2005 ordinance (Wikipedia), and Infraero's 2025 figures show 6,148,384 scheduled domestic passengers against 77 scheduled international ones (all arrivals, so probably diversions). The 2023 decisions were about limiting its traffic, which is a later claim.

claims.claim: federal limit on passenger numbers since 2024
claims.inAfter: A federal limit on passenger numbers has applied since 2024
claims.note: New, in place of 'Since 2023 ... Galeão taking the international flights'. The limit followed the August 2023 decision to push flights to Galeão; it was replaced on 8 November 2023 by an annual cap of 6.5 million from 2024 (Wikipedia). Infraero's 2024 report blames the federal limit for a 46 per cent fall in Santos Dumont's passengers in 2024, and its 2025 report (June 2026) says the limit still shaped 2025. A travel guide updated in August 2026 says the ceiling has been raised to 8 million for 2026; that has no second source, so no figure is given.

claims.note: New: the old text did not say who runs it. The brief expected Aena, but Santos Dumont has NOT passed to Aena: DECEA's live entry names Infraero as operator, Infraero lists it among its 24 airports (June 2026) and on its live airport list, and Aena's January 2026 results name its 17 Brazilian airports (six in the north-east and eleven in the block with Congonhas) without Santos Dumont (saved under CGH as aena-2025-traffic). Infraero's shares are held by the federal government (the Union).

claims.claim: terminal designed by the Roberto brothers, opened 1945
claims.inAfter: Its original terminal, designed by the Roberto brothers and opened in 1945
claims.note: Was 'the passenger terminal begun in 1938 was designed by the MMM Roberto brothers after Paris Le Bourget'. Infraero names Marcelo and Milton Roberto and the 1945 opening by President Getúlio Vargas; Wikipedia adds Mauricio (MMM Roberto), so 'the Roberto brothers' covers both. The 1938 start and the Le Bourget model rest on Wikipedia alone. 'Original' because a new departures building opened in 2007 (Infraero); the 1945 building now handles arrivals (Wikipedia).
